title: With My Bitter Thoughts...
text:
With my bitter thoughts

and with all my misfortunes,

I will make your wedding bouquet,

which will not be of orange blossoms.


My eyes, which anguish

and continual vigil

set alight, will be two wilted

torches for your altar.


The weeping that from my grief

without pause is springing

will anoint your pure brow

as with holy water...


—Sir, do not grieve, your frown

hurts me like a reproach;

—How pale you are, my lord!

—It is that I spent a bad night,

love takes sleep from me...


—And you are leaving!...

—I am leaving, it is late,

they are waiting for me; the temple burns

like a sun! Soothe your pain,

sir, and God bless you!

—Damiana, may God keep you...
editorial_note: This first-line variant keeps the grief-made wedding bouquet and farewell dialogue used in the Damiana translation.

title: To Leonor
text:
Your hair is black as the wing

of mystery; as black as a gloomy

nevermore, as a farewell, as a "who knows!"

But there is something blacker still: your eyes!


Your eyes are two pensive magicians,

two sphinxes sleeping in the shadow,

two very beautiful enigmas... But there is something,

there is something more beautiful still: your mouth.


Your mouth, oh yes; your mouth, divinely made

for love, for the warm

communion of love, your young mouth;

but there is something better still: your soul!


Your gathered, silent soul,

of compassions as deep as the open sea,

of tendernesses so deep...

But there is something,

there is something deeper still: your dream!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the ascending sequence from hair to eyes, mouth, soul, and dream.

title: As the Spark Sleeps in the Pebble...
text:
As the spark sleeps in the pebble

and the statue in the clay,

in you sleeps divinity.

Only in a constant and strong pain,

at the shock, springs from the inert stone

the lightning of deity.

Do not complain, therefore, of destiny,

for what is divine within you

only arises thanks to it.

Endure, if possible, smiling,

the life that the artist goes on sculpting,

the hard blow of the chisel.


What do bad hours matter to you,

if each hour in your newborn wings

places one more beautiful feather?

You will see the condor in full height,

you will see the sculpture finished,

you will see, soul, you will see...
editorial_note: This first-line variant preserves the same sculptural image of pain releasing the divine spark.

title: What Use Is Philosophy to the Sad One!...
text:
What use is philosophy to the sad one!

Kant or Schopenhauer or Nietzsche or Bergson...

Metaphysical dabblings!


Meanwhile, my Ana,

you have died on me, and I still do not know

where my poor reason must search for you.

Metaphysical dabblings, pure theory!

No one knows anything of anything: better

than that poor confused and empty science,

the soul lights us, like daylight,

the secret instinct of eternal love!


There can be no abyss that this love does not plumb,

and I will find you. Where? I do not care where!

When? I do not care... but I will find you!

If I ask a sage, "What do I know!" he answers.

If I ask my soul, it tells me: "I know!"
editorial_note: The translation renders the coined refrain as 'metaphysical dabblings' and keeps the grief-driven argument against theory.

title: Oh Christ!
text:
"There is no longer any human pain that is not my pain;

no eyes now weep, no soul is anguished

without my being anguished and weeping;

now my heart is the faithful lamp of every vigil,

oh Christ!"


"In vain I search in the deep hiding places of my being

to find some hatred: no one can wound me now

except through pity and love. All are I, I am all,

oh Christ!"


"What do evils or goods matter! For me all are goods.

The rosebush has no thorns: for me it gives only roses.

Roses of passion? What does it matter! Roses of heavenly essence,

purple as the blood you shed for us,

oh Christ!"
editorial_note: The translation keeps the repeated prayer address and the mystical identification with every pain.

title: To See in All Things...
text:
To see in all things

the traces of the unknown Spirit;

to contemplate

without cease,

in the transparent mysterious nights,

the holy nakedness of the stars...

To wait!

To wait!

What? Who knows! Perhaps a future

and undreamed-of peace... Serene and strong,

to run that sublime

and portentous adventure of death.


Meanwhile, to love everything... and to love nothing,

to smile when there is sun and when there are mists;

to take care that on the harsh journey

the wings do not atrophy, nor any wave

of vile mire soil our feathers.


Soul: such is the best orientation,

such is the instinctive course

shown to us by an inner

star.
editorial_note: This first-line variant keeps the same spiritual itinerary of waiting, detachment, and the inner star.

title: It Is Well!
text:
Because I still contemplate radiant dawns

and there are roses, many roses, many roses

where the star of Bethlehem trembles,

and there are roses, many roses, many roses,

thank you, it is well!


Because in the afternoons, with subtle faintness,

the sun piously kisses my temple,

and still transfigures it with its ray:

thank you, it is well!


Because at night a voice calls my name

(the voice of someone I know!), and there is an Eden

hidden in the folds of my shadow:

thank you, it is well!


Because even evil in me is a gift from heaven,

since, as it undermines me, with rough zeal,

it also crumbles my prison;

because my first flight is already drawing near:

thank you, it is well!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the refrain as grateful acceptance and preserves the prison-to-flight movement.

title: My Secret
text:
My secret? It is so sad! I am lost

in love with a vanished being,

with a freed soul,

who for ten years was mine, and who has gone...

My secret? I will tell it in your ear:

I am in love with a dead woman!


Do you understand—you who seek the visible

transports, the real, the tangible

caresses of the woman who takes shape

for all your invincible desires—

that impossible of impossibles:

to adore a ghost?


Well, such is my life and such has it been

and will be!

If for me alone

her noble heart beat, now silent and frozen,

must I show myself ungrateful

and forget her, merely because she has departed,

and leave her, merely because she has died?
editorial_note: The translation keeps the whispered confession and the contrast between tangible desire and ghostly fidelity.
